slides.notes: Last lesson we learned that the BPU only runs quantized, compiled models — .bin on X5, .hbm on the S series. Once you have a model, how do you run it on the board? This lesson answers three questions: first, how one codebase supports four boards; second, what is inside a Sample and where the entry points are; third, how to run ResNet-18 on X5 and S100 and read the results.

slides.notes: Before we start, get the materials ready. The star of this lesson is RDK Model Zoo on GitHub — we use the main branch and the commit fixed for this lesson. The ResNet README and Python runtime guide live under samples. For concepts, go to the Resource Center. On the board you need login access and reachability to the D-Robotics artifact download site; git-clone the repo into the course folder under /tmp, then run from the repo. If the board cannot reach GitHub, clone on a PC and scp it over.

slides.title: Model Zoo
slides.heading: What ==Model Zoo== is
slides.lead: A collection of BPU model samples maintained by D-Robotics. The current delivery line is the main branch (repository VERSION 2.0.0).

cards.title: On-board inference code
cards.text: Python entry points with pre/post-processing ready.

cards.title: Conversion and evaluation
cards.text: conversion/ for conversion; evaluator/ for evaluation.

cards.title: One main line
cards.text: main is the unified line; rdk_x5 and rdk_s remain as historical branches.

slides.notes: First, what Model Zoo is. It is our collection of BPU model samples. Each Sample has converted models, on-board inference code, plus conversion recipes and accuracy evaluation. Boards used to have separate branches; now main is the unified line at VERSION 2.0.0. The historical per-board X5 and S-series branches are still kept.

slides.title: Repo map
slides.heading: ==Four places== in the repo
slides.lead: Every later step uses these four places.
head: What it holds
rows: All Samples, by domain: vision, speech, llm, robotics, vla
Shared utilities: image/label I/O, Runtime wrappers
Artifact manifests models.yaml (x5 / s) and platforms.json
Eval data and class names, e.g. imagenet_classes.names
slides.notes: Next, how the repo is laid out. samples holds every Sample, split by domain into vision, speech, llm, robotics, and vla. utils holds shared tools such as image/label I/O and Runtime wrappers. docs/release holds the artifact manifests — one for X5, one for the S series — plus platforms.json, which maps board identity to a target. datasets holds evaluation data and class names.

slides.title: Select target
slides.heading: One codebase, ==four boards==

scene.text: Code stays the same; only target and artifacts change

steps.caption: One Sample codebase, to run on four boards
Pass --target for the board; use auto to let the program detect it
auto: read board identity, match platforms.json to a target
x5: X5 .bin artifact
s100: S100 .hbm artifact
s100p: S100P .hbm artifact
s600: S600 .hbm artifact
Code stays the same; only target and artifacts change

slides.notes: Here is the key: one codebase on four boards. There is only one Sample codebase. You tell it which board with --target: x5, s100, s100p, s600, or auto. With auto, the program reads board identity and matches platforms.json to a target. Once the target is set, the artifact is set too: X5 uses the bayese .bin; S100 uses nashe .hbm; S100P uses nashm; S600 uses nashp. The code stays the same; only target and artifacts change.

slides.title: Artifact naming
slides.heading: Artifacts are named ==by board==
slides.lead: bayese / nashe / nashm / nashp in the filename are the march — they are not interchangeable.
head: ResNet-18 artifact (under model/)
slides.notes: Artifact names follow a clear pattern. bayese, nashe, nashm, and nashp in the filename map to each toolchain's march. X5 is bayes-e with a .bin extension; S100 is nash-e, S100P is nash-m, and S600 is nash-p — all .hbm, each in its own subdirectory. Each board uses its own artifact; S100P cannot use an S100 file. Also, model/ itself does not commit binaries — fetch artifacts with the download script.

slides.title: Find a Sample
slides.heading: First decide ==whether it works for you==
slides.lead: All three steps need no board — you can do them on a PC.

cards.title: List the release manifest
cards.text: `--list-models` lists artifact references in the manifest.

cards.title: Dry-run the selection
cards.text: `--dry-run` only resolves the selection; it does not load the model.

slides.notes: First learn how to tell whether a Sample works on your board. Step one: read the support matrix in the README — which targets ship which variants. Step two: run main.py with --list-models; no board needed, it lists artifacts in the manifest. Step three: add --dry-run to check your selection only — no model load, no on-board SDK. With --target auto it lists every published reference. All three steps work on a PC.

slides.title: Support matrix
slides.heading: How to ==read the support matrix==
slides.lead: Find your board's column: — means not published. Sources: ResNet rows from the Sample README; YOLOv8 Detect from the Model Zoo online catalog.
head: X5
S100
S100P
S600
slides.notes: How to read the support matrix. Take ResNet: ResNet-18 has published artifacts on all four boards; C++ covers only the S series — X5 has no C++ runtime. For YOLOv8 Detect, the Model Zoo online catalog lists it for X5, S100, S100P, and S600. Not every model covers all four boards, so before you start, confirm your board and model on the online catalog card tags or hardware filter.

slides.title: Directory skeleton
slides.heading: A Sample's ==six directories==
head: What it owns
What it owns
rows: Artifact fetch; no binaries checked in
Code that runs on the board
slides.notes: Open a Sample such as samples/vision/resnet — there are six directories. model handles fetching model artifacts; conversion holds export and quantization recipes (next lesson); runtime holds on-board code; evaluator measures accuracy on a dataset; test_data has inputs you can run directly; tests are regression tests. Each Sample README also uses fixed sections — learn one, and the others are easy to find.

slides.title: Unified interface
slides.heading: Entry point, args, ==model class==

scene.label: utils/py_utils: shared image/label I/O and Runtime wrappers

steps.caption: main.py is a thin entry point
cli.py owns args, artifact selection, listing, and dry-run
classify.py holds the ResNetClassifier model class
predict() calls three stages in order
preprocess: CPU resize, crop, convert to NV12
infer: hand the model to the BPU
postprocess: softmax, take Top-K
You get the classification result
Switch to detect/seg Samples — the interface names stay the same

slides.notes: Next, the Python under runtime. main.py is a thin entry: parse args, build the model, call predict, print results. Args, artifact selection, listing, and dry-run live in cli.py. Real inference is in classify.py's ResNetClassifier: predict calls preprocess, infer, then postprocess. Pre/post run on the CPU; infer goes to the BPU. Switch to a detect or seg Sample — the interface names stay the same.

slides.title: Artifact selection
slides.heading: How to ==pick the right artifact==
slides.lead: Three ideas decide which file actually runs.

cards.title: manifest
cards.text: One line per artifact under docs/release — URL and format come from it.

cards.title: asset-id and path
cards.text: asset-id is the manifest name; model-path is the local file — they must match.

cards.title: Pre-run check
cards.text: If target disagrees with detected hardware, it errors out.

slides.notes: How do you make sure the right file runs? Three ideas. First, the manifest under docs/release — one line per artifact; download URL and format come from it. Second, asset-id and model-path: asset-id is the full name in the manifest, model-path is the local file — they must be paired, because the filename alone does not reveal the input protocol. Third, the pre-run check: if the requested target disagrees with detected hardware, the program errors out instead of forcing a run.

slides.title: Input protocol
slides.heading: Two ==input protocols==
slides.notes: The same code can run on four boards also because pre-processing prepares data for the input protocol. X5 models have one packed-NV12 input — a 1-D uint8 buffer; a 224×224 image is 75,264 bytes. S-series models have two inputs, Y and UV split: Y is (1,224,224,1), UV is (1,112,112,2). You do not assemble this yourself; check tensors with model_info and the protocol with --dry-run.

slides.title: Part 03
slides.heading: Run it on the board
slides.sub: Once on X5, once on S100
slides.notes: Part 3: run it on the board.

slides.title: X5 prep
slides.heading: X5: identify the board, download the model
slides.notes: Start on X5. On the board, git-clone the repo into the course folder under /tmp and enter the repo root; then identify the board by reading soc_name — measured output is X5U; then download ResNet-18 with download.sh to get an ~11.08 MB .bin. Run all commands from the repo root. Keep the trailing 2>/dev/null when reading identity: X5 has no boardinfo, S100 has no socinfo.

slides.title: X5 run
slides.heading: X5: inspect the model, run the Sample
slides.lead: model_info for input tensors; --dry-run for the protocol; then run main.py.

note.p: Defaults: in-repo white_wolf.JPEG and ImageNet labels.

slides.notes: Step three: use model_info to inspect input tensors — X5 has a single NV12 input named data; the protocol, shown later with --dry-run, is packed_nv12. Step four: run main.py with --target x5 --variant 18 and the defaults — the in-repo white wolf image and ImageNet labels. The terminal prints Top-5; rank 1 is white wolf at 0.998090.

slides.title: S100 prep
slides.heading: S100: identify the board, download the model
slides.lead: Same command shape — only change target and the download argument.
slides.notes: On S100, the same two steps. Read soc_name — output is S100; pass s100 to download.sh and get an ~12.19 MB .hbm. The command shape does not change.

slides.title: S100 run
slides.heading: S100: inspect the model, run the Sample
slides.notes: model_info again: S100 has two inputs, data_y and data_uv; the protocol, shown later with --dry-run, is split_nv12. Run main.py with only --target changed to s100 and --variant still 18 — rank 1 is again white wolf at 0.998109.

slides.title: Read results
slides.heading: How to ==read the results==
slides.lead: Measured (X5U / S100): order matches the README. X5 Top-1 0.998090; S100 Top-1 0.998109.
head: Class
X5 score
S100 score
slides.notes: Reading the results. Each row has three fields: class is the ImageNet-1k index, label is the name, score is after softmax. Measured order matches the README: white wolf, timber wolf, ice bear, Arctic fox, Samoyed. X5 rank-1 score is 0.998090; S100 is 0.998109; both class 270. For accuracy, the README reference Top-1 on ImageNetV2 for ResNet-18 is 58.91% on X5, 58.79% on S100, and 59.35% for the float model.

slides.title: Four steps to run a Sample
slides.heading: Run a Sample in ==four steps==

scene.text: Switch boards: change only target and artifacts — the four steps stay

steps.caption: Step 1: download the artifact
Step 2: model_info for inputs/outputs
Step 3: run main.py
Step 4: read the Top-5
Switch boards: change only target and artifacts — the four steps stay

slides.notes: Compress today's work into four steps. First, download the artifact with target and variant. Second, use model_info for inputs and outputs. Third, run main.py with --target for the board. Fourth, read the results — white wolf ranks first in Top-5; compare with the README. Switch boards by changing only target and artifacts — the four steps stay the same.

slides.title: Part 04
slides.heading: Switch boards and pitfalls
slides.sub: What to change when you switch boards
slides.notes: Part 4: switch boards and pitfalls.

slides.title: Switch board
slides.heading: Switching boards changes ==three places==
slides.lead: Test image, label file, and other args stay put.

cards.title: target
cards.text: Change x5 to s100 / s100p / s600, or use auto.

cards.title: Download argument
cards.text: Change download.sh's first argument to match.

cards.title: Artifact path
cards.text: S-series artifacts live under s100/, s100p/, s600/.

slides.notes: Switching boards changes three places only. First, --target: x5 → s100 / s100p / s600, or auto. Second, download.sh's first argument, kept in sync. Third, S-series artifacts live under s100/, s100p/, s600/ — the path follows. Test image, label file, and other args stay put.

slides.title: Common pitfalls
slides.heading: ==Five== common pitfalls
slides.lead: When it will not run, check these five first.

items.text: Inference does not auto-download — fetch first
C++ defaults to zebra — add a flag for white wolf

slides.notes: Five common pitfalls. First, S100P cannot use S100 artifacts — different march. Second, if target disagrees with detected hardware, the program errors out. Third, older or slim images may lack PyYAML/Pillow — install with pip; both boards used here already had them. Fourth, inference does not auto-download — run download.sh first. Fifth, the S-series C++ run.sh defaults to a zebra image; add --test-img for white wolf.
